issues.issue: "Lessee to carry insurance policy" names no coverage type, amount, insured or carrier, so the schedule entry has no ascertainable content standing alone. A court would have to decide whether it adds anything to, or is measured by, the insurance paragraph of the lease.

The $1,400 monthly charge "for use of the ARP Protocols and consultation" cannot be squared with Section 5 of the License Agreement, which imposes a $1,400 monthly license fee, and with the Rent paragraph's "PROTOCOLS $16,800.00" (12 x $1,400). Whether these are one obligation or two separate $1,400 charges is left open.

The lessee is identified only as "the Clinic Operator" with the identifying block left blank/illegible, so the instrument does not say whether the Lessee is the individual signer or his clinic entity. The same blank recurs in Section 1.4 ("Licensee shall refer to ___") and in the License Agreement's opening paragraph.

The term is fixed both by reference to "the first day of the month following the date of shipment or delivery" and by Block A's stated "Lease/License Start Date," which are different dates. The handwritten "ONE YEAR" appended to the paragraph must also be reconciled with the "No. of Months: 12" entry in Block A.

Rent is payable monthly "the sum shown in Block B above," but Block B's Rental amount is blank and the paragraph instead states two aggregate figures, EQUIPMENT $68,250.00 and PROTOCOLS $16,800.00, so the monthly rental is not stated. The equipment figure also differs from the cover page's "Total Price $68,750.00."

The "PROTOCOLS $16,800.00" component of rent duplicates the $1,400 per month payable under Section 5 of the License Agreement and Block D, so the same money is charged as both rent and license fee. Whether the licensee owes one $1,400 monthly obligation or two is unresolved.

The parties' recital that this is a "True Lease" under UCC Article 2A sits against the transaction's own terms — a one-year term at a price equal to the full stated value of the equipment — so a court could be asked whether the label controls the characterization. The paragraph also fixes commencement "as provided by Paragraph 1," which itself gives two different start dates.

The promise that "Lessor shall repair defects to the equipment free of charge during the term" cannot be squared with the Loss and Damage paragraph, which says "Lessee shall keep the A.R.P Trainers in good repair and any repair shall be at the Lessee's cost" without the misuse/negligence qualifier. Who pays for a non-negligent repair is therefore answered twice, in opposite ways.

The blanket disclaimer is qualified only by "EXCEPT AS IS SPECIFICALLY PROVIDED HEREIN," leaving it to be construed whether the Warranty paragraph's free-repair promise survives it and whether "herein" reaches the License Agreement bound in the same instrument. Section 10.1 of the License independently preserves "THE EXPRESS WARRANTIES, IF ANY, MADE IN THE ARP WAVE LEASE AND LICENSE AGREEMENT."

The cap limiting Lessor's liability to "THE TOTAL AMOUNT OF RENT PAID" does not say whether it reaches claims arising under the License Agreement in the same instrument, where Section 10.2 instead bars consequential damages outright with no cap. The two limitation regimes must be read together to know what a licensee-lessee may recover.

The sentence "Lessee shall keep the A.R.P Trainers in good repair and any repair shall be at the Lessee's cost" contradicts the Warranty paragraph's promise that Lessor will repair defects free of charge unless caused by Lessee's misuse or negligence. Nothing in either paragraph subordinates one to the other.

The carve-out "except as provided in this Paragraph 13" is a mis-numbered internal cross-reference: this is the Loss and Damage paragraph, while paragraph 13 of the Lease is Assignment. The exception therefore points at nothing.

The hell-or-high-water obligation is qualified by "Except as otherwise expressly provided herein" and by termination "pursuant to the express provisions of this Lease," without identifying which provisions those are. Whether the Warranty and Default paragraphs fall within that exception is left to construction.

Coverage is to be "in form and amount and with companies approved by the Lessor" and for replacement value "as determined by the Lessor," giving no ascertainable standard and no stated amount for the Lessee to meet. The schedule entry "Tns.: Lessee to carry insurance policy" supplies none either.

The obligation to pay "all license fees, registration fees, assessments, charges and taxes" conflicts with the cover schedule, which states "Filing Fees Lessor to pay" and "Sales or Other Tax _ Included." Which allocation governs the same charges is not addressed.

The default trigger for a false representation refers to a "document or instrument furnished to the Lessee," when the remedies run in Lessor's favor and the parallel clause in Section 7.1 of the License reads "furnished to the Licensor." As written the Lessor may declare default on its own documents.

The paragraph directs that "the Licensee shall follow at all times the protocols licensed in conjunction with the equipment under a separate agreement," although the license is contained in this same instrument, and the Lease's Entire Agreement paragraph says this Lease is the whole contract. Which document supplies the governing protocols is left ambiguous.

The bar on permitting "the equipment or any part thereof to be used by anyone other than the Lessee or the Lessee's employees" cannot be squared with the definition of an ARP Wave Clinic as a facility "providing rehabilitative and physical training services to the public by use of the Systems." Use of the equipment on patients, or by non-employee contract practitioners required by Section 4.1, is prohibited on the face of this paragraph.

Lessor may assign "without notice to the Lessee," while Section 2.5 of the License conditions Licensor's release on assignment upon the Licensee being "afforded notice of such assignment by Licensor." The notice consequences of a single assignment of the combined instrument are stated inconsistently.

Interest is set at "the highest rate permitted by the laws of the state whose laws govern this Agreement, but not to exceed 8% per annum," leaving it unclear whether 8% is the rate or merely a ceiling below a lower statutory rate. The phrase "the state whose laws govern this Agreement" also requires resort to the Construction paragraph to be given content.

The setoff authorization is circular as written: Lessor may apply against "amounts owing Lessor hereunder any amounts which might from time to time be owed to Lessor or any affiliate of Lessor by Lessee," when a setoff right requires amounts owed by Lessor to Lessee. The direction of the offset is a mechanical error that changes the clause's meaning.

"This Lease constitutes the entire agreement between the parties hereto" cannot be squared with the Default paragraph's cross-default on "the License Agreement or any other agreement executed with ARP WAVE," nor with Section 8 of the License, which declares that document the entire agreement. Two integration clauses in one instrument leave open what the parties' whole contract is, and whether the 2010 and 2012 ARP agreements survive.

Venue is limited to "the Hennepin County, Minnesota, Federal or State District Court" only "for the enforcement of this Agreement," leaving open whether non-contract claims (trade secret, tort, or claims under the License Agreement) fall inside the clause. "Hennepin County ... Federal ... District Court" also names no existing federal court by its proper designation.

This paragraph permits notice "delivered personally, given by prepaid telegram or mailed first class," while Section 9 of the License requires notices to be sent by facsimile or overnight courier. The two notice regimes in one instrument prescribe mutually exclusive methods.

The narrowing/blue-pencil sentence appears only in the Lease, so whether it reaches the License Agreement's two-year non-compete in Section 4.6 — the provision most likely to be "so broad as to be unenforceable" — depends on treating the two documents as one instrument. Section 8 of the License contains no comparable severability term.

The Licensee is never named — the party line is blank — so the identity of the counterparty must be found outside the words of the agreement. The same blank appears in Section 1.4's definition of "Licensee" and in the Lease's reference to "the Clinic Operator."

This recital defines "System(s)" to include ARP Wave™ and the Ultra Fit Athletic Mastery Protocols, but the operative grant in Section 2.1 licenses only Accelerated Recovery Performance, In Balance Muscle Testing and Wave Site Protocols. A licensee could argue the recital's broader description of what "is being licensed to Licensee" controls the narrower grant.

The recital's statement that the license is subject to Licensor's "ongoing monitoring, revision, upgrading, customizing, updating and modification" in its sole discretion asserts a power that the operative terms grant only in part (Section 2.4 as to enhancements). Whether the recital creates an independent right of unilateral modification of the licensed Systems is open.

The definition ends with the open-ended catch-all "related programs, and related intellectual property" appended to named protocols, giving no boundary to what falls within "System(s)." The same catch-all is repeated inside the definition, so the enumerated protocols do not limit it.

"Rehabilitative and physical training services" is undefined and its boundary matters, because Section 4.1 forbids the clinic from performing "any other type of physical therapy, training or rehabilitative service." What conduct falls inside the licensed clinic activity and what is prohibited turns on the same undefined phrase.

"Licensee is granted no right, title or license to, or interest in, any ARP Trademarks" cannot be squared with Section 2.2, which gives Licensee the right to operate its clinic "under the business name of 'ARP Wave Clinic.'" Whether the licensee may use the mark as a trade name is answered both ways.

The definition of "Licensee" is blank — it "shall refer to" nothing — so the defined party is not identified anywhere in the License Agreement. Every obligation keyed to "Licensee" therefore depends on extrinsic proof of who contracted.
